title: Which Way Does It Run?
objective: After this level you can spot reverse causation, where the supposed effect is really the cause.
summary: Sometimes the supposed effect is the cause. Reversing causation is a false cause fallacy; checking which came first can rule a cause out.

cards.headline: Whenever the streets fill with umbrellas, it rains. Do umbrellas bring rain?
cards.body: Obviously not: the rain brings out the umbrellas. Put like that, it's a joke. But the same backwards step hides inside plenty of serious-sounding claims, and it's much harder to spot when you don't already know which way the arrow points.

cards.headline: Reversing causation
cards.body: Reversing causation means drawing a causal conclusion with cause and effect swapped. It's another false cause fallacy. A logic encyclopedia gives this example: every officer at one company owns a big boat, so if you want to become an officer, get a bigger boat. The arrow runs the other way. Being an officer brings the high income that buys the boat.

cards.headline: The chocolate, reversed
cards.body: Messerli raised this reading of his own chocolate data. Perhaps sharper minds lead to more chocolate, not the other way round: people with superior cognitive function might know more about dark chocolate's health benefits and eat more of it. He even noted that winning a Nobel Prize might trigger a burst of chocolate eating, though most likely a brief one.

mascot.line: People mix these up: coming first can't prove a cause, but coming second rules one out.

cards.headline: Check the order
cards.body: One clue helps a lot: a cause must come before its effect, since effects never come before their causes. So ask what came first. The boat, or the promotion? Timing alone can't prove a cause, as Level 43's rooster showed. But when the supposed cause turns out to come second, the timing rules it out.

cards.headline: Direction: checked

title: Just a Coincidence?
objective: After this level you can explain why, given enough chances, surprising coincidences are bound to happen.
summary: Given enough people and chances, astonishing coincidences are bound to happen somewhere. Diaconis and Mosteller called it the law of truly large numbers.

cards.headline: She won the New Jersey lottery twice. The paper said: 1 in 17 trillion.
cards.body: A woman's double win made the front page of The New York Times as a long shot. It sounds like fate, or a fix. Two statisticians later took the story apart and reached a far less spooky conclusion, and a far more useful one.

cards.headline: The law of truly large numbers
cards.body: In 1989 the statisticians Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller put it in one line: "With a large enough sample, any outrageous thing is likely to happen." When enormous numbers of people and events pile up over time, almost any astonishing event is bound to turn up somewhere. The surprise is real. The mystery usually isn't.

cards.headline: The wrong question
cards.body: That 1 in 17 trillion figure answered a not-very-relevant question: the chance that one ticket wins two particular draws. And she had bought multiple tickets, again and again. The question that matters is different. Out of the millions of people buying lottery tickets, will someone, somewhere, win twice? Asked that way, a double winner stops looking like a miracle.

cards.headline: Two questions for any uncanny event
cards.body: Diaconis and Mosteller named other sources of coincidences too. Some have a hidden cause, Level 44's third factor in disguise. Memory plays its part: notable events stick while humdrum ones are forgotten. And we count near misses as matches. So when something uncanny happens, ask: how many chances were there? And is something hidden behind it?

title: More Than One Cause
objective: After this level you can explain why most events have several causes and why blaming only one misleads.
summary: Most events need several causes at once, like the fire triangle's oxygen, heat and fuel. Mill called the cause the sum of the conditions; picking one as 'the cause' depends on your interest.

cards.headline: A dropped match starts a forest fire. So the match caused it. Right?
cards.body: Partly. That match could have landed on wet moss or bare rock and simply gone out. The fire needed more than a spark, and so do most events. Trouble starts when we pick one cause and call it the cause.

cards.headline: The fire triangle
cards.body: Firefighters learn a simple model: a fire needs three things at once, oxygen, heat and fuel. Remove any one and the flames stop. That's why firefighting tactics and equipment are built to take away one of the three. In the forest, the match brought the heat. The dry wood and the air did the rest of the work.

cards.headline: Mill: all the conditions together
cards.body: In A System of Logic, published in 1843, John Stuart Mill noticed a habit: people single out one condition, call it the cause, and call the rest mere conditions. Strictly speaking, he wrote, the cause is "the sum total of the conditions, positive and negative taken together." The spark, the dry wood and the air are all part of it.

cards.headline: Which one gets called the cause?
cards.body: An event can have several contributing causes, and which one we call the cause depends on what we're interested in. A fire crew might point to the dry season; an investigator, to a careless camper. Both can be right. The error is oversimplifying: treating a minor contributing factor as the major one, as if the others weren't there.

title: Necessary or Sufficient?
objective: After this level you can tell a necessary condition from a sufficient one.
summary: A necessary condition must be there (no Y without X); a sufficient one guarantees the result. Some conditions are needed together and enough together.

cards.headline: No key, no entry. But a key in your pocket won't open the door.
cards.body: You also have to walk up and turn it. That small gap, between what you need and what's enough, is one of the most useful distinctions in logic. It's also one of the easiest to mix up.

cards.headline: Necessary: no Y without it
cards.body: X is a necessary condition for Y when you can't have Y without X: take X away and Y is guaranteed not to happen. Having four sides is necessary for being a square. Oxygen is necessary for life. Requirements and prerequisites are usually necessary conditions. They must be met, but on their own they don't guarantee success.

cards.headline: Sufficient: enough on its own
cards.body: X is a sufficient condition for Y when X guarantees Y: if X is there, Y is too. Being a square is sufficient for having four sides. Notice the flip. Four sides is necessary for a square, but it isn't enough. And practice is necessary for becoming a good basketball player, but practice alone isn't sufficient. Talent and coaching, anyone?

mascot.line: Common mix-up: needed is not enough. Necessary means no Y without X; sufficient means X alone brings Y.

cards.headline: Needed together, enough together
cards.body: Air is necessary for a flame, but air alone lights nothing. Some conditions are individually necessary and jointly sufficient: peanut butter, jelly, bread and a knife are together enough for a PB&J, though none is enough alone. Confusing necessary with sufficient is all too common in everyday reasoning, so ask which one a claim really means.

title: When the Measure Becomes the Goal
objective: After this level you can explain Goodhart's law: why a number stops measuring well once people are rewarded for hitting it.
summary: Goodhart's law: a number stops measuring well once people are rewarded for hitting it. Goodhart said it in 1975; Strathern's 1997 wording made it famous.

cards.headline: Imagine a reading contest: one sticker per book. Watch the thin books vanish.
cards.body: Nobody cheats, exactly. The children simply do what the contest rewards. The count of books shoots up, but it stops telling you how much anyone is reading. There's a law for this, and it started in economics.

cards.headline: Goodhart's law
cards.body: In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart was writing about monetary policy, where officials steered by targets for growth in the money supply. He put the problem this way: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." In plain words: a number that tracks something well can stop tracking it once people push on it.

cards.headline: The famous wording isn't his
cards.body: The version most people quote came later. In a 1997 paper on audits in British universities, the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern summed it up: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." What began as a jocular aside became a widely applied idea, far beyond economics.

cards.headline: Why the number breaks
cards.body: A measure is only a sign of what you want. Reward the sign, and people find cheaper ways to produce it. Judge scholars by how many papers they publish, and you encourage "salami slicing": dividing the findings of one study into many separate papers. Quantity wins over quality. The count rises; the science doesn't. People respond to incentives.

title: Milestone: Reasons, Evidence and Causes
objective: After this level you can connect arguments, evidence and causes into one method for checking a claim.
summary: John Snow's 1854 case against the Broad Street pump, taken apart with the first half of the tree: an argument, a best explanation, a straw man to avoid, converging evidence and a claim about cause.

cards.headline: Milestone: London, 1854. Cholera kills 500 people in 10 days.
cards.body: Most doctors blamed the air. Halfway to Mastery, here's one real case that uses everything so far: an argument, the evidence behind it and a claim about cause. The doctor John Snow suspected the water. Watch how he built his case, and where it was weaker than the legend.

cards.headline: A cluster on the map
cards.body: Doctors then thought disease spread by breathing dirty air, called miasma. Snow took the addresses of the dead and plotted the cases on a map. The deaths clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. That's a correlation, and an argument: the premise, deaths cluster around the pump; the conclusion, the pump's water is spreading the disease.

cards.headline: The brewery that stayed well
cards.body: A cluster alone could hide another cause, so the useful evidence is people near the pump who didn't drink from it. A brewery stood on Broad Street, near the pump. Of more than seventy workmen, none had cholera in a severe form; only two were even mildly unwell. The brewery had its own deep well, and the men were allowed malt liquor. Same street, different water, almost no cholera.

cards.headline: The handle, and a caution
cards.body: Snow met the parish Board of Guardians on 7 September 1854, and the pump handle came off the next day. Legend says that ended the outbreak. But Snow himself wrote that attacks had already fallen before the handle was removed. Credit the handle alone and you'd commit Level 43's post hoc fallacy. The strong evidence was the pattern, not the timing.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway there
learned: How to take an argument apart into its premises, hidden assumptions and conclusion.
Why induction and best-explanation reasoning give likely answers, not certain ones.
How a fallacy like the straw man knocks down a view nobody actually holds.

How to test a causal claim, and why a link can come from a hidden third factor or mere timing.

title: Looking Only for Yes
objective: After this level you can explain confirmation bias and counter it by looking for evidence that could prove you wrong.
summary: Confirmation bias favors information that fits your beliefs. Bacon's votive tablets show it: count the hits, forget the misses. The counter: hunt for evidence that could prove you wrong.

cards.headline: A temple wall of paintings from sailors who survived. Proof the gods listen?
cards.body: Sailors caught in storms made vows, and those who escaped shipwreck hung up paintings to give thanks. In 1620 Francis Bacon retold what one visitor asked when he was shown the wall and pressed to admit the power of the gods. His question still works today.

cards.headline: Where are the drowned?
cards.body: The visitor asked: where are the portraits of those who drowned in spite of their vows? The wall showed only the hits. Bacon saw the same pattern far beyond the temple. Believers in omens and dreams, he wrote, note the events that come true and pass over the failures, though the failures are much more common. Once the mind adopts a view, it draws everything else in to support it.

cards.fact: Confirmation bias: looking for, or reading, information in ways that fit what you already believe.
cards.context: Today we call Bacon's pattern confirmation bias. It has two moves: seeking evidence for your view, and not seeking evidence against it, or giving that evidence too little attention. Suppose you think your friend Sam is always late. Every late arrival sticks in your mind. The on-time days never get counted at all.

mascot.line: Keep this: before you count the yeses, go looking for a no.

cards.headline: The counter: go looking for a no
cards.body: Bacon's fix: when you test a rule, the negative instance is the most powerful one. One sailor who prayed and drowned tells you more than a wall of survivors. Britannica gives the same advice for everyday life: consciously seek out information that contradicts your beliefs. You can think of counterexamples; the trouble is you're not motivated to. So ask: if I were wrong, what would I expect to see? Then go and look. Count Sam's on-time days too.

cards.headline: Confirmation bias: spotted
learned: Bacon's wall showed hits, not misses
Confirmation bias favors what you already believe
One solid "no" can outweigh many "yeses"
Ask what you'd see if you were wrong, then look

title: Believing What We Want
objective: After this level you can explain motivated reasoning: starting from the answer you want and working backward to reasons.
summary: Motivated reasoning starts from the conclusion you want and builds reasonable-looking reasons for it. Gilovich's two questions show the moving bar. Caring about accuracy helps.

cards.headline: Your team loses on a last-second call. The replay looks clear to you.
cards.body: Fans of the other team watch the same replay and see the opposite, just as clearly. None of them feels like a cheat. Each feels they are simply looking. This level is about how a wish can steer your reasoning without ever announcing itself.

cards.headline: Sneakier than wishful thinking
cards.body: Wishful thinking is blunt: it's true because I hope it is, and a hope is no reason at all. Motivated reasoning is subtler. In 1990 the psychologist Ziva Kunda reviewed the evidence: people are more likely to reach the conclusions they want, but only as far as they can build seemingly reasonable justifications for them. So you don't skip the reasons. You start from the answer and work backward to them.

cards.headline: Two different questions
cards.body: Psychologist Tom Gilovich captures the trick in two questions. For a conclusion we want, we ask, "Can I believe this?" For one we don't want, we ask, "Must I believe this?" The second sets a much higher bar. The bar moves, and it never feels as if it moved. As Nicholas Epley and Gilovich put it, the result is biased beliefs that feel objective.

cards.headline: The counter: care about being right
cards.body: Kunda's review also points to a way out. A goal of reaching one particular conclusion favors the reasoning strategies most likely to deliver it. A goal of being accurate favors the strategies that are most appropriate. So first notice which answer you are hoping for. Then put the same question to both sides: must I believe this? If one side only ever has to pass "Can I?", you've found the wish at work.

cards.headline: Motivated reasoning: spotted
learned: Motivated reasoning works backward from a wanted answer
It builds reasons, so it feels objective
"Can I believe it?" versus "Must I believe it?"
Aim for accuracy: ask "Must I?" of both sides

title: The Double Standard
objective: After this level you can use the switch-sides test: would you accept this argument if it backed the opposite conclusion?
summary: A double standard judges alike cases by different rules; special pleading exempts the case you care about. The switch-sides test asks whether you'd accept the same argument for the other side.

cards.headline: Your sister takes the last slice: greedy. You take it: you were hungry.
cards.body: Same act, two verdicts. From the inside, each verdict can feel perfectly fair. That's what makes this trap so hard to catch in yourself, and why this level ends with a test instead of a promise to do better.

cards.headline: One ruler, not two
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy names the error plainly: when two cases should be judged by the same standard and you use different standards, your reasoning uses a double standard. A close cousin is special pleading: applying a principle everywhere except the one case that interests you. "Everyone should return library books on time. Mine was late for a good reason, though."

cards.headline: You've met this already
cards.body: Level 52's two questions are a double standard for evidence. A conclusion you like only has to pass "Can I believe this?" One you dislike has to pass "Must I believe this?" Same kind of evidence, two different bars. And each bar, taken alone, looks reasonable. That's why double standards hide so well.

cards.headline: The switch-sides test
cards.body: The fix is a procedure. Ask: would I accept this argument if it backed the opposite conclusion? In 1984 psychologists Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston found that getting people to consider the opposite reduced bias more than telling them to be as fair and unbiased as possible. They traced the problem to a failure Bacon had noticed: not considering possibilities at odds with what you believe right now.
cards.callout: Trying to be fair is a wish. Switching sides is a check.

cards.headline: Double standards: caught
learned: A double standard uses two rulers for alike cases
Special pleading exempts the case you care about
Switch sides: would you accept it the other way?
Considering the opposite beat "be fair" in tests

options.label: When an argument relies on two or more premises
options.rationale: Most arguments have several premises; that's fine.

options.label: When alike cases are judged by different standards

options.rationale: Updating on evidence isn't a double standard.

options.label: When two people disagree about the answer
options.rationale: Disagreement alone isn't the fallacy.

questions.explanation: Lord, Lepper and Preston found considering the opposite reduced bias more than instructions to be fair: it's a check, not a wish.

options.label: It lets you pick whichever side you prefer
options.rationale: The point is to judge both sides by one rule.

options.label: It proves your original view was wrong
options.rationale: It checks your standard, not your conclusion.

options.label: It's a concrete check: same argument, other side
It avoids looking at evidence at all
options.rationale: It makes you weigh the evidence twice, once per side.

questions.explanation: Same kind of evidence, two different bars: that's a double standard, applied to evidence.

options.label: the switch-sides test
options.rationale: That's the cure, not the problem.

options.rationale: Nothing is left unsaid; two bars are in use.

options.label: a fair way to weigh evidence
options.rationale: Fair weighing uses one bar for both.

title: Natural Isn't Always Better
objective: After this level you can spot the appeal to nature: assuming something is good or safe just because it is natural.
summary: The appeal to nature says natural means good and unnatural means bad. Its hidden premise fails: the death cap is natural, and natural supplements carry real risks.

cards.headline: "All natural!" says the label. What is that supposed to prove?
cards.body: It sounds like a promise. But read it again: the label never says the product is safe, or that it works. It leaves you to fill that in yourself. This level is about the gap it leaves you to fill.

mascot.line: This is Level 7's move in a new place: find the premise nobody said, then check it.

cards.headline: The premise nobody says
cards.body: The appeal to nature runs: it's natural, so it's good. Or its mirror: it's unnatural, so it's bad. Remember Level 7's unstated premise, the one an argument needs but never says? Here it's "whatever is natural is good". Say it out loud and it wobbles. There's a second problem: "natural" is vague, and it often works as a loaded word that slips in praise instead of describing anything.

cards.fact: The death cap is a wild mushroom, and the deadliest mushroom known to humans.
cards.context: It causes most of the world's fatal mushroom poisonings. Nobody made it in a lab; it's as natural as anything gets. As the Fallacy Files puts it, poisonous plants and animals are as natural as any other living thing, and nobody recommends eating them. So "natural, therefore good" fails on its very first test.

cards.headline: Natural isn't a safety rating
cards.body: The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says it directly: "natural" does not always mean safe. Kava belongs to the pepper family, yet kava supplements can cause liver disease. The herbal supplement St. John's wort makes many medicines less effective. None of this makes natural things bad. It makes "Is it natural?" the wrong question. Ask what the evidence says about this thing, wherever it came from.

cards.headline: Appeal to nature: spotted
learned: "Natural, so good" hides a premise
"Natural" is vague and often loaded
The death cap is natural and deadly

questions.explanation: Like Level 7's hidden premises, the argument only works if whatever is natural is good. Said out loud, it's easy to doubt.

options.rationale: Price has nothing to do with the argument.

options.rationale: The argument doesn't rely on that.

options.rationale: That's the mirror form; this argument needs the positive one.

title: Perfect or Nothing
objective: After this level you can spot the perfect-solution fallacy: rejecting an idea because it doesn't solve the whole problem.
summary: The perfect-solution fallacy rejects a real improvement because it isn't total. Seat belts cut deaths by about half. Demsetz's fix: compare real options, not reality with an ideal.

cards.headline: "Seat belts don't save everyone. So why bother wearing one?"
cards.body: Said out loud, it sounds silly. Yet the same shape of argument turns up everywhere: a spelling checker is useless because it misses some typos; a new bike lane is pointless because some cyclists will still ride in traffic. This level names the pattern and gives you one question that deflates it.

cards.fact: Seat belts cut serious crash injuries and deaths by about half.
cards.context: That's the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's figure. About half is not all, so some people wearing belts still die in crashes. "Not all" is exactly the gap the hook's argument pounces on, as if a huge improvement counted for nothing because it isn't total.

cards.headline: The perfect-solution fallacy
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls it the perfectionist fallacy: rejecting a proposal solely because it doesn't solve the problem perfectly, in cases where perfection isn't really required. It also goes by the perfect solution fallacy or the nirvana fallacy. The hidden rule is "if it isn't perfect, it isn't worth doing". Notice the fine print, though: sometimes perfection really is required. A lock that works most days isn't much of a lock.

cards.headline: Compared with what?
cards.body: In 1969 the economist Harold Demsetz criticized what he called the nirvana viewpoint: find gaps between the ideal and the real, then conclude the real is failing. He urged comparing real alternatives instead, and economists now call the mistake the Nirvana fallacy. That gives you the question that deflates it: compared with what? Not belts against a crash nobody gets hurt in. Belts against no belts.

cards.headline: Perfect-or-nothing: spotted
learned: Rejecting a fix for not being total is a fallacy
Also called the nirvana fallacy
Seat belts cut deaths by about half
Always ask: compared with what?

title: Sounding Sure Isn't Evidence
objective: After this level you can explain why a confident, fluent delivery is not a reason to believe a claim.
summary: Confidence persuades because it often goes with knowledge, but it can be sent without any. Style isn't substance, and a bare assertion isn't an argument, however loud.

cards.headline: Two friends give directions. "Left. Definitely." "Um, left, I think?"
cards.body: Which friend do you follow? The sure one sounds more persuasive, and that isn't an accident. This level is about why confidence persuades, and why the way a claim is said can feel like evidence when it isn't.

cards.headline: Why confidence persuades
cards.body: Researchers call the shortcut the confidence heuristic: people are confident when they know they're right, and their confidence makes them persuasive. That's why the shortcut exists. Often the sure-sounding friend really does know the way. The trap is that the signal can be sent without the knowledge behind it. Anyone can say "definitely".

cards.headline: Style isn't a premise
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy lists a fallacy called style over substance: taking the style of an argument as adding to its strength. A salesperson's smile and sharp clothes add nothing to their reasons. Level 2 gave you the rule already: asserting a view, however heatedly, isn't giving an argument. Volume, polish and certainty are how a claim is said, not a reason to believe it.

cards.headline: Sure and wrong
cards.body: In a 2007 study, Elizabeth Tenney and colleagues found that confident witnesses were judged more credible than unconfident ones. But errors damaged the confident witnesses' credibility more. After a mistake, the less confident witness could seem the more believable one. So treat confidence as a claim about knowledge, and check it: ask for the reason, and remember who has been sure and wrong before.

title: Patterns in Noise
objective: After this level you can spot the Texas sharpshooter fallacy: drawing the target around the bullet holes after the fact.
summary: The Texas sharpshooter draws the target after shooting, making chance look like skill. Cancer cluster investigators guard against it by setting their definitions first.

cards.headline: Fire at a barn, then paint the bull's-eye around the holes. Great shot?
cards.body: Every shot is a bull's-eye if you draw the target afterward. That picture gave its name to a real reasoning error, the Texas sharpshooter fallacy, and it hides wherever people go looking for patterns after the fact.

cards.headline: Targets drawn afterward
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy says the fallacy comes from overemphasizing random results, or making selective use of coincidence. Its example: Psychic Sarah makes 26 predictions for the year. When one of them comes true, she says she can see into the future. The misses quietly vanish, and the one hit becomes the bull's-eye.

cards.headline: Clusters that aren't
cards.body: Cancer is common, so cases can appear to cluster even when they have no connection at all. That's why CDC guidance warns investigators about the Texas sharpshooter: notice the cases first, then draw the "affected" area around them, and a link appears that may be nothing but chance. In one review of US cancer cluster investigations over 20 years, a clear cause turned up in just one case.

mascot.line: Keep this: decide what counts as a hit before you look, never after.

cards.headline: Draw the target first
cards.body: The same CDC guidance gives the cure: investigators must set out their definitions, assumptions and methods before they look. The habit works anywhere. Decide what counts as a hit before the evidence comes in. Think your lucky socks win games? Pick the games you'll count before the season starts, not after the wins.

learned: The sharpshooter draws the target after shooting

title: The Bias Blind Spot
objective: After this level you can explain why people spot bias in others far more easily than in themselves.
summary: People see bias in others far more readily than in themselves, because they judge themselves by their thoughts and others by their behavior. Intelligence doesn't shrink the blind spot.

cards.headline: Quick: are you more biased or less biased than the average person?
cards.body: If you said "less", you're in large company. In surveys, people rate themselves as less subject to biases than the average American. They can't all be right. This level is about why the answer feels so obvious from the inside.

cards.fact: People see bias far more readily in others than in themselves.
cards.context: Psychologists Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin and Lee Ross called this the bias blind spot in a 2002 paper. Notice the twist. Every trap in this chapter so far, you can probably spot in a friend. Spotting it in yourself is the hard part.

cards.headline: Why you can't see it
cards.body: When you judge yourself, you look inward, at your thoughts and intentions, and they seem fair. But bias often works outside awareness, so looking inward finds nothing. When you judge others, you look at what they actually do. There's a second reason: your own view feels like a plain view of reality, so people who see things differently seem to be the biased ones.

cards.headline: Smarter isn't safer
cards.body: You might hope intelligence helps. In a 2012 study, Richard West, Russell Meserve and Keith Stanovich found that higher cognitive ability did not shrink the blind spot; if anything, it went with a larger one. What did help, in a 2007 study, was learning how much of judgment runs outside awareness. The habit: judge yourself by your behavior, the way you'd judge anyone else.

title: "We've Always Done It This Way"
objective: After this level you can spot the appeal to tradition and explain when a long track record is, and isn't, a good reason.
summary: Bloodletting lasted from antiquity to the 1800s without working as claimed. The appeal to tradition treats 'we've always done it' as proof; Chesterton's fence says find the reason first.

cards.headline: From ancient times until the 1800s, doctors drained blood from the sick.
cards.body: Bloodletting was meant to balance the body's "humors", fluids once thought to govern health. Generation after generation of doctors used it. Surely a treatment trusted for that long must work?

cards.headline: What the track record hid
cards.body: Being used for centuries is not the same as being tested. When the physician Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis studied the results, publishing first in 1828, he found bloodletting was not as effective as its supporters claimed. Even then, tradition let go slowly: some medical textbooks still recommended it as late as 1942.

cards.headline: The appeal to tradition
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls it the fallacy of traditional wisdom: saying a practice must be fine today simply because it was the apparently wise practice in the past. Note the careful word simply. The encyclopedia grants that a tradition is some reason, just not always a good enough one, for instance when conditions have changed. "We've always done it this way" can start a conversation. It can't end one.

cards.headline: Chesterton's fence
cards.body: So when does a track record count? In his 1929 book The Thing, G. K. Chesterton imagined a fence across a road. A reformer who says "I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away" should first go and find out its use. A tradition may hold a reason nobody remembers. Find the reason, then judge it on its merits, as Louis did with bloodletting.

title: Checkpoint: Traps in Our Reasoning

summary: Feynman's first principle, don't fool yourself, ties the chapter together. Each trap has a habit that counters it: hunt for the no, switch sides, draw the target first, ask compared with what.

cards.headline: Richard Feynman's first rule for thinking: don't fool yourself.
cards.body: The physicist gave that advice to new Caltech graduates in 1974, and added that you are the easiest person to fool. Nine levels of traps later, you know exactly why. Let's line them up.

cards.headline: Leaning over backwards
cards.body: Feynman described scientific integrity as a kind of utter honesty, a leaning over backwards. If you do an experiment, report everything that might make it invalid. If you put out a theory, put down the facts that disagree with it as well as those that agree. That's Bacon's negative instance, turned into a rule for honest work: the misses get counted along with the hits.

title: What Makes Science Different
objective: After this level you can explain science as a way of testing ideas against the world and correcting its own mistakes.
summary: Science works only with testable ideas and lets evidence, not reputation or tradition, decide. Abderhalden's nonexistent enzymes show how others' checks catch false claims, even fraud.

cards.headline: A famous scientist's pregnancy test. One snag: the enzymes weren't there.
cards.body: In the early 1900s, the influential physiologist Emil Abderhalden announced that the body makes protective enzymes that could reveal a pregnancy. Other scientists tried his test and couldn't reproduce his results. UC Berkeley's Understanding Science calls it fraud. So how does science catch a false claim when the person making it is famous?

cards.headline: Testable: the entry ticket
cards.body: Science works only with ideas that can be tested using evidence from the natural world. A testable idea tells you what you should see if it's true, and what would count against it. Abderhalden's enzymes passed that first bar: if they existed, his test should work on real patients. An idea that fits every possible observation can't be tested at all, so science can't get a grip on it.

cards.headline: Evidence outranks reputation
cards.body: In science, whether an idea is accepted depends on the evidence for it, not on dogma, popular opinion or tradition. Ideas the evidence doesn't support are eventually dropped, however grand their author. That's how the enzymes fell. Other scientists ran the test, couldn't reproduce the results, and the enzymes turned out not to exist. A famous name couldn't save them.

cards.headline: Built to catch its own mistakes
cards.body: Scientists get things wrong like everyone else. The difference is the system around them. Science's habit of scrutiny, with other scientists checking and re-running each other's work, helps uncover errors, and the ongoing process regularly corrects wrong turns. A mistake can survive for a while. It just can't hide from the next test forever.

title: Could It Be Proved Wrong?
objective: After this level you can explain Karl Popper's idea that a scientific claim must be falsifiable.
summary: Popper's test: a scientific theory must clash with some possible observation. Einstein's risky light-bending prediction passed it; theories that fit any behaviour could not.

cards.headline: "Tomorrow it will rain, or it won't." Never wrong. Never useful.
cards.body: A forecast that no weather could prove wrong tells you nothing about the weather. The philosopher Karl Popper turned that simple thought into a test for science itself.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: "falsifiable" doesn't mean false. It means a test could show it false, if it were.

cards.headline: Popper's test
cards.body: Karl Popper, an Austrian-British philosopher who lived from 1902 to 1994, asked what makes a theory scientific. His answer was falsifiability: a scientific theory must clash with some possible observation. It has to stick its neck out and say, in effect, "If you ever see this, I'm wrong." A theory that no observation could ever contradict fails the test.

cards.headline: Einstein bet on bending light
cards.body: Popper admired Einstein's theory of relativity because it made a risky prediction: light bends towards massive bodies. If careful measurements had shown no bending, the theory would have been in serious trouble. In 1919, Eddington's observations bore it out. That's Popper's point: evidence for a theory counts only when it comes from a prediction that might have failed.

cards.headline: The theory that explains everything
cards.body: Popper saw the opposite in the psychoanalytic theories of his day. They could account for any human behaviour at all, so no conceivable observation could contradict them. Admirers counted that as a strength. Popper counted it as a weakness: like the forecast of rain or no rain, a theory that fits every outcome makes no real prediction.

title: Hypothesis, Prediction, Test
objective: After this level you can explain the logic of a scientific test: a hypothesis predicts something, and a failed prediction counts against it.
summary: A hypothesis predicts what we should observe; a mismatch counts against it. Rutherford's gold-foil surprise sank the spread-out atom. A passed test supports an idea but doesn't prove it.

cards.headline: Fire tiny particles at gold foil. A few come flying back.
cards.body: That surprise, in Ernest Rutherford's lab, overturned the picture of the atom. It only counted as a surprise because someone had first worked out what ought to happen.

cards.headline: Idea first, then a prediction
cards.body: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation, reasoned from what's already known. It isn't a wild guess. Testing it takes two steps. First: if the idea is correct, what would we expect to see? Second: does that match what we actually observe? A match supports the idea. A mismatch counts against it.

cards.headline: The snowball atom
cards.body: Before 1910, Rutherford, like many scientists, pictured an atom's positive charge and mass spread evenly through it, like a loosely packed snowball. The prediction followed: alpha particles fired through gold foil should pass with only minor scattering. Most did. But some bounced back, as if they had hit something dense. The prediction failed, so the snowball had to go. Rutherford concluded the atom has a dense core: a nucleus.

cards.headline: Passing isn't proving
cards.body: The two outcomes aren't equally final. A mismatch counts against an idea, as the gold foil showed. A match supports it, but the next test could still go the other way. That's why science neither proves nor disproves ideas once and for all. It accepts or rejects them on the evidence, and stays ready to revise the verdict.

title: A Theory Isn't a Guess
objective: After this level you can explain what scientists mean by a theory, and why "just a theory" misunderstands the word.
summary: Everyday "theory" means a hunch; a scientific theory is a broad explanation backed by many lines of evidence, like atomic theory or gravity. Theories never graduate into laws.

cards.headline: "It's just a theory." Would you say that about gravity?
cards.body: People say it to wave an idea away. But the word "theory" means something very different in a lab than it does over dinner, and mixing up the two meanings turns a compliment into a put-down.

cards.headline: One word, two meanings
cards.body: In everyday talk, a theory is a hunch: "My theory is the dog ate the cake." In science, a theory is a powerful explanation for a broad set of observations, and to be accepted it has to be backed by many different lines of evidence. So "it's just a theory" swaps the scientific meaning for the everyday one.

cards.headline: What theories look like
cards.body: Atomic theory, gravity and plate tectonics are all theories in the scientific sense: broad explanations that tie together huge ranges of observations, each supported by multiple lines of evidence. Nobody drops a pen and wonders whether gravity is only a hunch. Calling something a theory is how science names its biggest explanations.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time: theory and law aren't ranks on a ladder. They're different kinds of claim.

cards.headline: Theories don't graduate
cards.body: A popular picture says a hypothesis grows up into a theory, and a theory into a law, as evidence piles up. It doesn't work that way. Hypotheses, theories and laws differ in breadth, not in how well supported they are. A theory isn't a law in waiting. It's already the big explanation.

title: Saving a Theory at Any Cost
objective: After this level you can spot an ad hoc rescue: an excuse invented only to protect a claim from evidence against it.
summary: An ad hoc rescue adds an excuse whose only job is to dodge the evidence. Le Verrier's unseen planet was a fair rescue: it made a new prediction, and Neptune was there.

cards.headline: "My lucky socks always work. Today? I wore them inside out."
cards.body: Every loss gets its own excuse, and the socks stay lucky forever. It sounds silly with socks. The same move turns up with ideas far more serious than socks, and it's worth knowing on sight.

cards.headline: The ad hoc rescue
cards.body: When a prediction fails, you can always save an idea by adding something that makes it fit the facts. Karl Popper, of Level 62, called such an add-on merely ad hoc when its only purpose is to dodge the evidence. The idea survives, but it has stopped sticking its neck out. "Inside out" explains one lost game and predicts nothing else.

cards.headline: Not every rescue is a cheat
cards.body: Adjusting a theory isn't always cheating; Popper came to accept it as a normal, respectable part of science. Take Uranus, which didn't travel exactly as astronomers expected. Urbain Le Verrier proposed an unknown planet tugging on it and worked out where it should be. In 1846, Johann Galle looked there and found Neptune on his first night of searching.

mascot.line: Keep this: a fair rescue makes a new bet. An ad hoc rescue only explains away the loss.

cards.headline: The test: does the rescue risk anything?
cards.body: Here's the difference. Le Verrier's rescue made a new prediction that could have failed: a planet, right about there. The inside-out excuse can never be checked against anything. So ask of any rescue: does it make a new, checkable claim, or does it only protect the old one?

title: When You Can't Experiment
objective: After this level you can explain how scientists showed that smoking causes lung cancer without experimenting on people.
summary: Unable to experiment ethically, Doll, Hill and others compared patients, followed British doctors forward from 1951, and weighed Hill's viewpoints such as temporality.

cards.headline: You can't make people smoke for decades to see who gets sick.
cards.body: An experiment like that would be unethical. Yet the case that smoking causes lung cancer was made anyway, by reasoning carefully from what could be observed. How?

cards.headline: Testing without an experiment
cards.body: Some ideas can't be tested by experiment, because it would be unethical. Scientists can still work out what a hypothesis predicts and check it, just as Level 63 described. If smoking causes lung cancer, lung cancer patients should turn out to be smokers more often than other patients. Studies around 1950, including Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's, compared patients and concluded smoking was "a cause, and an important cause" of the disease.

cards.headline: Then follow people forward
cards.body: Comparing patients after they fall ill is one check. A stronger one follows people forward. In 1951 a study of British doctors recorded their smoking habits, then followed their causes of death for 50 years. By 1954 it had already confirmed the extra lung cancer among smokers. Because the habits were recorded before anyone fell ill, the smoking plainly came first.

cards.headline: Hill's viewpoints
cards.body: In 1965 Hill set out nine viewpoints for judging whether a link is causal, among them strength, consistency, dose-response (more exposure, more disease) and temporality: the cause comes before the effect. Temporality is perhaps the only one epidemiologists all agree is essential. Hill never meant them as a checklist. They're questions that, together, turn many observations into one strong case.

title: Peer Review
objective: After this level you can explain what peer review checks before a study is published, and what it can miss.
summary: Editors send a study to other scientists in its field, who check its reasoning and evidence before publication. It is a filter, not a guarantee: Hwang's fabricated cloning claims got through.

cards.headline: Before a study reaches a journal, other experts try to pick it apart.
cards.body: The journal asks them to. It's called peer review, and it's one of science's main quality checks. It catches a lot. It doesn't catch everything.

cards.headline: How it works
cards.body: Scientists write up a study and send it to a journal. The editors pass it to several other scientists who work in the same field: the peers. They send back criticism and tell the editor whether they think it's good enough to publish. Often the authors revise and try again.

cards.headline: What reviewers check
cards.body: To be accepted, an article must meet science's standards: build on other work in the field, rely on logical reasoning and well-designed studies, and back up its claims with evidence. In Level 1's terms, reviewers are sorting good arguments from bad before the rest of us read them.

cards.headline: A filter, not a guarantee
cards.body: Peer-reviewed work isn't necessarily correct. Woo Suk Hwang published a claim that his lab had cloned human embryos and collected stem cells from them. Scientists scrutinizing his data later spotted duplicated graph peaks, the claim turned out to be fabricated, and his papers were retracted. Publication isn't where checking ends; it's where the wider checking begins.

title: How Science Changes Its Mind
objective: After this level you can explain how new evidence overturned accepted ideas, such as bacteria causing most stomach ulcers.
summary: In 1982 ulcers were blamed on stress and lifestyle. Warren and Marshall found a bacterium, Marshall infected himself, and cures that killed the bacteria settled it: a Nobel Prize in 2005.

cards.headline: In 1984 a doctor infected himself on purpose.
cards.body: Barry Marshall's results were widely disbelieved, so he made himself the test subject. His story shows how science changes its mind: slowly, then for good.

cards.headline: What everyone knew
cards.body: In 1982, stress and lifestyle were considered the major causes of peptic ulcers. Then pathologist Robin Warren noticed curved bacteria in stomach samples, always near inflammation. Marshall grew the unknown bacterium in the lab, and together they found it in almost all patients with stomach inflammation or ulcers. The accepted idea had a rival.

cards.headline: Evidence that wouldn't go away
cards.body: Marshall infected himself with the bacteria and developed stomach inflammation. Treatment studies did the rest. Ulcers healed by cutting stomach acid kept coming back, but patients were cured once the bacteria were wiped out. Today a short course of antibiotics and acid inhibitors can cure an ulcer.

cards.headline: How the mind changed
cards.body: Helicobacter pylori is now firmly established as the cause of most ulcers: more than 90% of duodenal ulcers and up to 80% of gastric ones. In 2005 Marshall and Warren won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The switch took years, and that's normal: changing an accepted theory is a community process, and good ideas aren't always recognized right away. What finally tipped it was the evidence.

title: Spotting Pseudoscience
objective: After this level you can spot pseudoscience by its untestable claims and its habit of moving the goalposts.
summary: Pseudoscience is non-science posing as science. Two questions expose it: could its claims fail, and what do its promoters do when a test goes against them?

cards.headline: A bracelet that "rebalances your energy field." Lab-inspired. Quantum-tuned.
cards.body: It sounds as if a lab made it. But sounding scientific and being scientific are different things. Two questions tell them apart, and neither needs a lab.

cards.headline: Science in costume
cards.body: Many writers describe pseudoscience as non-science posing as science: it isn't scientific, but its promoters try to make it look that way. It can borrow the whole costume, with conferences, journals and associations that share science's surface features but not its quality standards. Remember Level 6's misleading "so"? The word alone proves nothing; the job it does is what counts.

cards.headline: Question one: could it fail?
cards.body: One philosopher's list of warning signs includes an unwillingness to test, ignoring results that go against the theory, and tests arranged so the theory can only be confirmed, never disconfirmed. An "energy field" that no instrument could ever detect fails Level 62's test before it starts: there's no observation that could count against it.

mascot.line: Be kind to people and tough on claims. Ask: could it fail? And what happens when it does?

cards.headline: Question two: what happens after a miss?
cards.body: Many pseudoscientific claims have in fact been tested, and failed. What gives them away is the reply. Instead of accepting the result, promoters move the goalposts: they change the requirements after the attempt, so success always stays out of reach. "It only works if you believe in it." That's Level 65's ad hoc rescue, used again and again.

title: Checkpoint: How Science Tests Ideas
objective: After this level you can explain how controls, blinding, randomizing and replication turn a hunch into knowledge.
summary: Semmelweis tested explanations of childbed fever by their predictions: birth position failed, handwashing succeeded. Modern trials add controls, randomizing, blinding and replication.

cards.headline: The 1800s: on one maternity ward, new mothers keep dying of fever.
cards.body: A doctor there, Ignaz Semmelweis, watched an unusually high share of new mothers die of what was called childbed fever. He had a list of possible explanations. How he sorted them is this whole chapter in one story.

cards.headline: Suspect one: the birth position
cards.body: Each explanation was a hypothesis, and each made a prediction. If giving birth lying on the back caused the fever, having women labor on their sides should lower it. Semmelweis tried it. The fever didn't fall. The prediction failed, so the evidence counted against that idea, exactly as Level 63 describes.

cards.headline: Suspect two: the doctors' hands
cards.body: Doctors often came straight from autopsies to women in labor. If their unclean hands carried the fever, thorough washing with a strong disinfectant should cut it. When Semmelweis made them wash, fever rates plummeted. The prediction could have failed, Level 62 style, and it didn't. That's strong support, though not final proof.

cards.headline: Guarding the test
cards.body: Modern tests build in more protection. In many medical trials, people are randomly assigned to a treatment group or a control group, and blinding keeps them from knowing who got which, to reduce bias. Then other researchers try to replicate the result. A finding nobody can repeat, like Abderhalden's enzymes, doesn't last.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: How a scientific test works: a hypothesis predicts, and a failed prediction counts against it.

title: Three Ways to Persuade
objective: After this level you can identify appeals to character, emotion and reason: Aristotle's ethos, pathos and logos.
summary: Aristotle sorted persuasion into three kinds: the speaker's character (ethos), the hearer's emotions (pathos) and the argument itself (logos). Only logos is an argument you can check.

cards.headline: Three ways to sell you an umbrella on a cloudy day
cards.body: The shopkeeper can remind you she has sold umbrellas for years. She can make you picture your good shoes soaked through. Or she can show you the forecast. Three different kinds of pull, and Aristotle sorted persuasion into exactly these three. His list still works.

mascot.line: Keep this: ethos is the speaker, pathos is the listener, logos is the argument. Three places to look.

cards.headline: Character, feeling, argument
cards.body: In his Rhetoric, Aristotle said persuasion comes through three means: the character of the speaker (ethos), the emotional state of the hearer (pathos), or the argument itself (logos). The shopkeeper's years behind the counter are ethos. Your soggy shoes are pathos. The forecast is logos. One pitch can use all three, so the useful skill is telling them apart.

cards.headline: Ethos: why should I trust you?
cards.body: Persuasion by character works when the speech makes the speaker seem worth believing. Aristotle named three things that inspire that confidence: good sense, good moral character and goodwill toward the audience. His twist: it has to be done by what the speaker says, not by what people thought of them beforehand. Credibility is earned in the speech itself.

cards.headline: Pathos: the mood changes the verdict
cards.body: Aristotle noticed that our judgments when we're pleased and friendly are not the same as when we're pained and hostile. A judge who feels friendly toward the accused thinks they did little wrong; a hostile judge thinks the opposite. That's why speakers stir feelings: feelings shift judgment. Same facts, different mood, different verdict.

cards.headline: Logos: the argument itself
cards.body: The third means persuades through proof, or apparent proof, in the words of the speech. It's the only one of the three built like Level 5's arguments, with premises and a conclusion. Notice the word "apparent": logos can be a bad argument dressed up well. Checking which it is, is logic's job.

title: Appeals to Emotion
objective: After this level you can tell when emotion is relevant to a decision and when it stands in for the reasons.
summary: Emotion in an argument isn't a fallacy. The appeal to emotion is: accepting a claim just because it stirs feelings, or letting feelings replace the key premises.

cards.headline: Max broke his wrist in the big game. Should he get an A in history?
cards.body: You'd feel for him. Anyone would. But a broken wrist, however sad, says nothing about what Max wrote on the quiz. That gap is this level's subject: when a feeling is part of the reasons, and when it's standing in for them.

cards.headline: Feelings aren't the fallacy
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy is clear that there's nothing wrong with using emotions when you argue. The fallacy is accepting a claim merely because an appeal stirs your anger, fear, pity or pride. Pitying Max's misfortune is proper. Giving him an A because of it is the appeal to pity.

mascot.line: Keep this test: take the feeling away. If a reason is still standing, the argument never needed the feeling to work.

cards.headline: Relevant, or replacing?
cards.body: Emotions go wrong, the same source says, when they serve as an argument's key premises or as tools to downplay relevant information. So ask whether the feeling is about the very thing being decided. Fear of a cliff edge is relevant to where you walk. Pity for Max is not relevant to what he scored.

cards.headline: The courtroom trick
cards.body: Matthew Knachel's logic textbook describes a lawyer who spends the closing speech on a client's suffering instead of proving the other side was at fault. That's why it files the appeal to emotion under fallacies of distraction. Even when the suffering is real, it pulls your attention away from whether the premises support the conclusion.

title: Loaded Words
objective: After this level you can spot how word choice, like "used" versus "pre-owned", tilts a claim before any argument is made.
summary: Word choice can deliver a verdict before any argument: firm or pig-headed, used or pre-owned. Loaded language slips a value judgment into what looks like description.

cards.headline: "I am firm. You are obstinate. He is a pig-headed fool."
cards.body: Bertrand Russell offered this "conjugation" on the BBC radio program the Brains Trust, and in 1948 a magazine ran a contest for more. All three describe the same stubbornness. Only the verdict changes, and it arrives before anyone has given a reason.

cards.headline: Used, or pre-owned?
cards.body: Dictionaries define pre-owned simply as secondhand, or used. Same car, same mileage, gentler word. That's a euphemism: an agreeable word swapped in for one that sounds harsh or unpleasant. Nothing about the car changed on the lot. Only how you feel about it did.

cards.headline: Loaded language
cards.body: Loaded language is emotive wording that expresses a value judgment. Slipped into what looks like plain description, it can lead you to adopt that value when no good reason has been given. "The reckless new skate park opens Friday" reads like news. "Reckless" is a verdict riding along for free.

mascot.line: It connects: a loaded word is Level 4's value judgment wearing a fact's clothes. Undress it and you can question it.

title: Same Fact, Different Frame
objective: After this level you can explain framing: why "90 percent survive" and "10 percent die" feel different but say the same thing.
summary: "90 percent survive" and "10 percent die" say the same thing, yet the gain frame is judged more favorably. Flip the frame before you decide.

cards.headline: Surgery A: 90 percent survive. Surgery B: 10 percent die. Which one?
cards.body: Most people lean toward A; it sounds safer. Now read them again. They describe exactly the same operation. Nothing differs but the wording, and the wording still pulls.

cards.headline: The framing effect
cards.body: Researchers call this framing. Describing the same information as a gain (a 90 percent survival rate) or as a loss (a 10 percent mortality rate) can change people's judgments, and the gain version is judged more favorably. Nothing in the facts moved. Only the spotlight did.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: framing isn't lying. Both frames are true. The trick is which truth gets the spotlight.

cards.headline: One claim, two sentences
cards.body: If 90 percent survive, the other 10 percent don't. So the two descriptions are equivalent: one is true exactly when the other is. In Level 3's terms, they make the same claim. A frame can't change whether a claim is true. It can only change which part of it you notice.

cards.headline: Flip the frame
cards.body: The habit that beats it is simple: before you decide, restate the claim in the opposite frame. "90 percent survive" becomes "10 percent die". "Nine in ten dentists agree" becomes "one in ten doesn't". Same information both ways. If your feeling flips with the wording, the wording was doing the persuading.

title: Weasel Words
objective: After this level you can spot vague words like "up to" and "helps" that make a claim sound bigger than it is.
summary: Weasel words like "up to" and "helps" make a claim sound big while promising almost nothing. Ask for the version you could check.

cards.headline: The sign shouts "70% OFF!" Squint, and there's a tiny "Up to".
cards.body: One logic textbook uses exactly this shop window. For all you know, one unloved item at the back is 70% off and everything else barely budges. Two small words turned a promise into a ceiling.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the date. Remember the egg: a weasel word looks full and holds nothing.

cards.headline: Why weasels?
cards.body: Merriam-Webster defines a weasel word as one used to evade a direct statement. The name comes from old lore that a weasel could suck out an egg and leave the shell intact: it looks fine but it's empty. Real weasels can't manage it. Weasel words can. The term's first known use was in 1900.

cards.headline: "Up to" on trial
cards.body: In 2012 the US Federal Trade Commission released a study of ads for replacement windows promising "up to 47%" savings on energy costs. Many consumers believed they would get the full 47%. The FTC's view: if you say "up to", you should be able to show people are likely to get that result under normal conditions.

cards.headline: Make it checkable
cards.body: Other weasels are quieter. "Helps fight plaque" dodges a direct statement: it doesn't say how much, for whom or compared with what, so almost no result could prove it wrong. The fix is to ask for the version you could check. How much? For whom? By when? A claim that can't lose can't tell you much either.

title: The Loaded Question
objective: After this level you can spot a loaded question that smuggles in an assumption you never agreed to.
summary: A loaded question builds in an assumption, so any direct answer admits it. Don't answer it straight: reject it, or split it into parts.

cards.headline: "Will that be cash or card?" You never said you were buying.
cards.body: Some salespeople are taught to ask exactly this. Two options, and both end in a sale, because the question has already settled the part you were still deciding: whether to buy anything at all.

cards.headline: What's hiding in the question
cards.body: A loaded question carries a false or questionable presupposition, so any direct answer implies it. Try "Have you stopped cheating at Monopoly?" Say yes, and you used to cheat. Say no, and you still do. Either way, you've admitted something nobody proved.

cards.headline: A claim in disguise
cards.body: Level 3 said questions can't be true or false. A loaded question exploits that: it sneaks a claim into the conversation without ever asserting it, so there's no statement on the table to challenge. A claim you can see, you can deny; this one never shows itself. And if you refuse a simple yes or no, you can be made to look evasive.

mascot.line: It connects: the hidden claim works like Level 7's unstated premise. Say it out loud, and you can finally question it.

cards.headline: Defusing it
cards.body: The right move is not to answer directly but to reject the question. Some parliamentary rules even allow "dividing the question" into simpler parts. Split it: "Have you ever cheated at Monopoly?" comes first. If the answer is no, the second question never arises.

title: One Word, Two Meanings
objective: After this level you can spot equivocation, where an argument quietly switches the meaning of a key word halfway through.
summary: Equivocation switches the meaning of a key word partway through an argument. Pin down the word's meaning in every premise and in the conclusion.

cards.headline: "Brad is a nobody. Nobody is perfect. So Brad is perfect."
cards.body: Each step sounds fine, and the ending is absurd. The trick is one word doing two jobs. The first "nobody" means an unimportant person. The second means no person at all.

cards.headline: Equivocation
cards.body: Equivocation is switching the meaning of a word that appears twice in the same reasoning: one word, taken two ways. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls the switch illegitimate, and it happens without warning, which is why it can be hard to spot. Brad's argument only works if you don't notice "nobody" changing jobs.

cards.headline: Bats and banks
cards.body: Some words carry unrelated meanings under one spelling: a bat that flies and a bat you swing, a bank for money and a river bank. Take "All banks are beside rivers, so my bank is beside a river." Read "bank" as riverside, and the conclusion about your bank doesn't follow. Read it as the money kind, and the premise is false.

mascot.line: People mix these up: to equivocate in everyday talk means to dodge. In logic it means one word quietly changing meaning.

cards.headline: Puns are innocent
cards.body: Ambiguity alone isn't a fallacy. Most words have more than one meaning, and context usually settles which is meant. Equivocation becomes a fallacy when the switch makes a bad argument look good. The fix: pin down the key word's meaning in each premise, then check it still means the same thing in the conclusion.

title: No True Scotsman
objective: After this level you can spot the move that redefines a group to wave away a counterexample.
summary: Antony Flew's Scotsman rescues a generalization by redefining the group after a counterexample. The claim survives but becomes true by definition and says nothing.

cards.headline: "No Scot would do such a thing!" Then came the news from Aberdeen.
cards.body: In a story told by the philosopher Antony Flew, a Scotsman reads about a shocking crime in an English town and declares that no Scot would do such a thing. Soon he reads of something worse, done by a man in Aberdeen. His reply: "No true Scotsman would do such a thing!"

cards.headline: The move
cards.body: Flew named the fallacy after that story. It's a rescue: faced with a counterexample to a generalization, the speaker redefines the group so the counterexample no longer counts. The claim survives, but only because the rules changed after the evidence came in.

mascot.line: It connects: Level 4's factual claims can be checked. Once a claim is true by definition, there's nothing left to check.

cards.headline: True, and empty
cards.body: "No real fan leaves early" sounds like news about fans, something you could test at any stadium. After the rescue, anyone who leaves early isn't a real fan, so the claim is true by definition. It gains truth and loses information: now it tells you only how the speaker uses the word "fan".

cards.headline: Warning signs
cards.body: Watch for "true", "real" and "genuine" in front of an ordinary noun: true fans, real cooks, genuine gamers. A strict definition can be fair, but it should be set out before the counterexample shows up. A standard invented afterward is just moving the goalposts. So ask before you look: what would count against this claim?

title: Persuasion or Manipulation?
objective: After this level you can tell persuasion that gives you good reasons from manipulation that works around them.
summary: Rational persuasion gives you reasons; coercion forces you; manipulation works around your judgment through trickery or pressure. Feelings alone don't make it manipulation.

cards.headline: Irving wants Tonya to choose X. His reasons didn't work. Now what?
cards.body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy opens its entry on manipulation with this pair. Irving could charm Tonya, make her feel guilty, nag her, or stoke a fear until X looks better. Each tactic, the entry says, could reasonably be called manipulation.

cards.headline: Three ways to change a mind
cards.body: Philosophers usually set manipulation apart from two other kinds of influence. Rational persuasion gives you reasons. Coercion forces you. Manipulation is neither. One view pictures a scale of pressure: persuasion exerts none, coercion the most, and manipulation sits somewhere in between.

cards.headline: Around your judgment, not through it
cards.body: Accounts of manipulation fall into rough families. One says it bypasses your reasoning. Another treats it as trickery, planting misleading beliefs or associations. A third sees pressure: guilt trips and nagging make saying no costly. What they share is the route. Persuasion goes through your judgment; manipulation goes around it.

mascot.line: People mix up Level 72 and this one. That was about arguments. This is about the route: through your judgment, or around it.

cards.headline: Feelings aren't the dividing line
cards.body: Philosophers find it implausible that every appeal to emotion is manipulative. So the test isn't whether you felt something. Ask instead: is this giving me a reason I could check, or pushing me to decide before I can? Taking time to weigh the grounds is Level 1's suspended judgment, put to work.

title: Checkpoint: Persuasion and Rhetoric

summary: A school-board mascot speech, taken apart: ethos, pathos, a loaded word, a loaded question and a weasel word, around one real reason. Techniques don't make a case wrong; judge the reasons.

cards.headline: A school board must pick a new mascot. Dana has two minutes.
cards.body: Dana wants the Hawks to replace the Snails. Her speech is rhetoric in the plain sense: communication meant to change how others see things. Let's take it apart with this chapter's tools and see what's left when the techniques are set aside.

cards.headline: Dana's speech

Up to half the students already wear Hawks shirts. And in last spring's survey, most students picked the Hawks." Aristotle would spot ethos in the first line and pathos in the second. Only one line is a reason.

So spotting a technique doesn't make Dana wrong. Set the techniques aside, weigh the survey that's left, and the Hawks may still deserve to win.

title: When to Trust an Expert
objective: After this level you can tell real expertise from a false appeal to authority, such as an expert speaking outside their field.
summary: Trusting experts is usually good reasoning. An appeal to authority fails when the expert is outside their field or the real authorities disagree, as Linus Pauling's vitamin C claims show.

cards.headline: Linus Pauling won two Nobel Prizes, all to himself. Trust him on colds?
cards.body: Pauling won the 1954 Chemistry prize for research on the chemical bond, then the 1962 Peace Prize: no one else has won two unshared. In the 1970s he concluded that vitamin C would prevent and ease the common cold, and vitamin C became widely used against colds. When someone that brilliant speaks, does that settle it?

cards.headline: Trusting experts is usually good reasoning
cards.body: You can't test every claim yourself, so you trust your dentist about teeth and a pilot about flying. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy says most appeals to authority are not fallacious: much of our knowledge properly comes from listening to authorities. So "an expert says so" is often a perfectly good reason. The real question is when it stops being one.

mascot.line: Keep this: before you ask "expert or not?", ask "expert in what?"

cards.headline: When an appeal to authority fails
cards.body: The same encyclopedia lists the warning signs. The person isn't really an authority on this subject. They can't be trusted to tell the truth. They've been misquoted. Or the real authorities disagree. Its example: a film star selling a watch is an authority on acting, not on watches. Fame, and even genius, doesn't follow you into a new field.

Pauling was a theoretical physical chemist, and his vitamin C views were never widely accepted by the medical establishment. title: Who Benefits?
objective: After this level you can weigh a conflict of interest without dismissing a claim just because of who made it.
summary: A conflict of interest is a secondary interest, like money, that may sway judgment about a primary one. It calls for disclosure and a closer look at the evidence, not for dismissing the claim.

cards.headline: A study says Sparkle toothpaste whitens best. Sparkle paid for the study.
cards.body: Your first thought might be: well, of course it did. That instinct is half right. Knowing who benefits is useful. But on its own it can't tell you whether the study is wrong. This level is about holding both thoughts at once.

cards.headline: What a conflict of interest is
cards.body: The International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) defines it carefully. A conflict of interest exists when professional judgment about a primary interest, such as the validity of research, may be influenced by a secondary interest, such as financial gain. Money is the easiest kind to spot, but rivalries and strong intellectual beliefs can count too. Notice the word "may": a conflict is a risk, not a verdict.

cards.headline: Why journals ask for disclosure
cards.body: The ICMJE says a relationship doesn't always mean a paper was badly influenced. Its answer is transparency: readers must be able to make their own judgments, and that takes full disclosure. So the Sparkle study should say, plainly, who paid for it. Then you can decide how hard to look.

mascot.line: "Who benefits?" is a reason to look closer. It's never a reason to stop looking.

cards.headline: The trap on the other side
cards.body: Throwing the study out just because Sparkle benefits is its own mistake. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy files it under attacks on the person: pointing to an arguer's vested interest doesn't undermine the reasoning, which should stand or fall on the evidence. So ask the next question. What exactly did the study measure, and how?

cards.headline: Interests: weighed
learned: A conflict of interest is a risk, not a verdict
Money is common, but rivalries count too
Disclosure lets readers judge for themselves
Who benefits? Look closer; don't stop looking

title: Straight From the Source
objective: After this level you can tell a primary source from a secondhand retelling and explain why details drift as a claim is passed on.
summary: A primary source reports firsthand; a secondary source retells. "Let them eat cake" drifted from Rousseau's unnamed princess and her brioche to Marie Antoinette and cake.

cards.headline: "Let them eat cake": Marie Antoinette's famous line. She probably never said it.
cards.body: That's Britannica's verdict: probably not. So where did the line come from, and how did it end up in her mouth? Following it back is a lesson in how claims change as they are passed along.

cards.headline: Firsthand or secondhand?
cards.body: Librarians sort sources by how far the author stands from the event. A primary source reports firsthand, or is the first record made right after: a diary, a letter, a photograph. A secondary source conveys the experiences and opinions of others. It's secondhand. Each retelling is one more step away from what actually happened.

cards.headline: Back to an early telling
cards.body: One of the earliest known versions is in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Confessions, written in the 1760s. Rousseau recalls "a great princess" who, told the peasants had no bread, said to let them eat brioche. He never names her. Marie Antoinette was a child at the time, so it's unlikely she was the princess he had in mind.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the dates. Remember the move: when a quote sounds perfect, go and find the first place it appears.

cards.headline: How the story drifted
cards.body: The earliest known source tying the line to the queen appeared in 1843, in the French journal Les Guepes, more than 50 years after the French Revolution. Along the way two details changed. An unnamed princess became a famous queen, and brioche, a rich bread made with eggs and butter, became cake. Nobody had to lie. Each retelling just leaned on the one before.

cards.headline: Sources: traced
learned: Primary sources are firsthand; secondary retell
Each retelling is a step further away
Rousseau's princess was unnamed, and ate brioche
The link to Marie Antoinette came in 1843

title: Consensus and the Lone Dissenter
objective: After this level you can explain why a field's consensus usually outweighs one contrarian expert, and how consensus can still change.
summary: A consensus is what survives many experts checking each other, so it usually outweighs one contrarian. Wegener's continental drift shows a consensus can change, when new evidence arrives.

cards.headline: In 1912, a weather scientist said the continents move. Geologists said no.
cards.body: The German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift, and it was not well received: scientists firmly believed continents and oceans stayed put. He turned out to be broadly right. So should you always back the lone rebel? The story says something more interesting.

cards.headline: Why a consensus weighs more
cards.body: Scientists check each other's work: they review it, try to repeat it and look for flawed reasoning. UC Berkeley's Understanding Science adds that a diverse community balances out individual biases. So a consensus isn't a headcount. It's the view still standing after many independent checks. One contrarian has passed only their own.

cards.headline: The lone voice on the news
cards.body: Understanding Science warns about false balance: presenting different scientific views as equal when the evidence strongly favors one side. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy draws the same line. When authorities genuinely disagree, leaning on any one of them is weak, but the occasional lone wolf doesn't make a field divided.

cards.headline: Wegener's weak spot
cards.body: Wegener had real clues: the fit of South America and Africa, and matching fossils on both coasts. But he couldn't say what force could move continents. The geophysicist Harold Jeffreys argued, correctly, that solid rock couldn't plow through the ocean floor. The skeptics weren't just being stubborn. They were pointing at a real gap.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: "a consensus once changed" doesn't mean "ignore consensus". It changed because of evidence.

cards.headline: What changed the consensus
cards.body: Wegener died in 1930 on a Greenland expedition, his theory still disputed. From the 1950s, new evidence from the ocean floor revived his ideas and led to plate tectonics, now widely accepted. The consensus moved when the evidence did, not when someone argued louder.

cards.headline: Consensus: weighed
learned: A consensus survives many experts' checks
False balance treats unequal views as equal
Wegener's drift lacked a force to move continents
Ocean-floor evidence changed the consensus
